Both used military power and coerced labor to control colonial populations.
Both were Protestant imperial powers.

differences.entityA: Britain eventually controlled a much larger territorial empire,
differences.entityB: Dutch power was concentrated mainly in Indonesia and nearby trading posts.

differences.entityA: British colonial expansion centered heavily on India
differences.entityB: Dutch colonial expansion centered on the Dutch East Indies.

differences.entityA: The British East India Company initially expanded through treaties with local rulers
differences.entityB: the Dutch frequently used violent suppression to remove local rulers and monopolize trade.

differences.entityA: The Dutch Culture System required farmers to devote approximately one-fifth of their land to export crops or provide corvée labor.
differences.entityB: Dutch Empire did not share this distinguishing feature to the same extent.

differences.entityA: British territories produced a wider range of goods, including cotton, tea, opium, and rubber.
differences.entityB: Dutch territories concentrated on tea, rubber, sugar, and spices, sometimes reducing land available for rice

differences.entityA: Britain established numerous settler colonies
differences.entityB: the Dutch Empire remained more focused on trade and resource extraction.

differences.entityA: The Dutch East India Company eventually went bankrupt, after which the Dutch government assumed direct control of its territory
differences.entityB: Dutch Empire did not share this distinguishing feature to the same extent.

similarities.claim: Both were Catholic colonial empires and spread Catholicism through missionaries.
Both controlled colonies in the Americas and Caribbean.
Both relied on plantation cash crops and African chattel slavery.
Both developed syncretic cultures and religions through interactions among Europeans, Africans, and Indigenous peoples.
In both empires, enslaved people could sometimes obtain freedom through manumission.
Both faced major colonial independence movements.

differences.entityA: Spain conquered large territorial empires with dense Indigenous populations
differences.entityB: France controlled a mixture of smaller settlements, trading territories, plantation colonies, and resource-extraction colonies.

differences.entityA: Spain relied heavily on silver mining, especially at Potosí
differences.entityB: France relied more on sugar, coffee, fur, palm oil, rubber, rice, and opium.

differences.entityA: Spain used encomienda, hacienda, and modified mit’a labor
differences.entityB: France relied more on chattel slavery, indentured servants, and later colonial cash-crop labor.

differences.entityA: French territories did not use the same detailed system throughout their empire.
differences.entityB: Spanish territories developed the formal castas hierarchy

differences.entityA: France depended on alliances with Indigenous peoples for the North American fur trade
differences.entityB: Spanish officials more often directly conquered, taxed, and forcibly converted Indigenous communities.

differences.entityA: major French colonies such as Algeria and Vietnam remained under French control until the twentieth century.
differences.entityB: Most Spanish American colonies gained independence during the early nineteenth century

differences.entityA: The Haitian Revolution abolished French rule and slavery in Saint-Domingue
differences.entityB: Spanish American revolutions were generally led by wealthy creoles and produced more socially conservative governments.

similarities.claim: Both were Catholic Iberian empires that spread Christianity through missionaries.
Both followed mercantilist policies.
Both claimed overseas territory under the Treaty of Tordesillas.
Both relied on African chattel slavery and plantation agriculture.
Both traded sugar, silver, enslaved people, and other colonial goods.
Both developed racially mixed colonial societies in which manumission was sometimes possible.

differences.entityA: Spain controlled most of the Americas west of the Treaty of Tordesillas line
differences.entityB: Portugal controlled Brazil and territories to the east in Africa and Asia.

differences.entityA: Spain built a largely land-based empire by conquering the Aztec and Inca civilizations
differences.entityB: Portugal initially created a trading-post empire along African and Asian coasts.

differences.entityA: Spain’s colonial economy depended heavily on silver mining
differences.entityB: Portugal depended more heavily on the spice trade, slave trade, and Brazilian sugar.

differences.entityA: Spain used encomienda, hacienda, and modified mit’a labor
differences.entityB: Portugal relied especially heavily on enslaved plantation labor in Brazil.

differences.entityA: Spanish society developed the formal castas system
differences.entityB: Portuguese colonies generally had more flexible racial categories and greater use of manumission.

differences.entityA: Spain governed extensive American territories through centralized colonial administrations
differences.entityB: Portugal’s early empire consisted mainly of forts and coastal trading posts.

differences.entityA: Portuguese Asian power declined as the Dutch and British captured important trading centers,
differences.entityB: Brazil remained Portugal’s most important colony

similarities.claim: Both were influenced by Enlightenment ideas such as natural rights, popular sovereignty, and representative government.
Both experienced revolutions that challenged monarchy and inherited privilege.
Both created written declarations of rights and constitutional governments.
Both industrialized and became major military and economic powers.
Both acquired territories outside their original borders and participated in imperialism.
Both fought with the Allies during World Wars I and II.
Both became permanent members of the United Nations Security Council and founding members of NATO.

differences.entityA: The American Revolution was a colonial independence movement against Britain,
differences.entityB: the French Revolution was an internal social and political revolution against France’s monarchy and estate system.

differences.entityA: The United States established a relatively stable federal republic
differences.entityB: France repeatedly shifted between republics, constitutional monarchies, empires, and restored monarchies.

differences.entityA: United States did not share this distinguishing feature to the same extent.
differences.entityB: France provided crucial military assistance to the American Revolution, but the cost worsened France’s debt and helped cause the French Revolution.

differences.entityA: the American Revolution preserved many existing inequalities, including slavery.
differences.entityB: The French Revolution abolished feudal privileges and attempted broader social restructuring

differences.entityA: slavery continued in the United States until the Civil War.
differences.entityB: France abolished slavery during its revolution, although Napoleon later restored it in French colonies

differences.entityA: The United States industrialized rapidly after the Civil War and became a leading producer of steel, oil, and automobiles
differences.entityB: France industrialized more slowly.

differences.entityA: The United States emerged from World War II as a global superpower,
differences.entityB: France’s global influence declined as colonies such as Vietnam and Algeria gained independence.

similarities.claim: Both gained independence through revolutions against European colonial powers.
Both revolutions were influenced by Enlightenment principles and ideas about natural rights.
Both created constitutions and independent governments after their revolutions.
Both revolutions inspired later independence movements.
Both received or sought foreign alliances during their struggles.

differences.entityA: The United States revolted against Britain,
differences.entityB: Haiti revolted against French colonial rule.

differences.entityA: The American Revolution was led mainly by property-owning colonists
differences.entityB: the Haitian Revolution was led largely by enslaved and formerly enslaved people.

differences.entityA: The United States preserved slavery after independence
differences.entityB: Haiti permanently abolished slavery and established equal citizenship in its constitution.

differences.entityA: The United States gained French assistance,
differences.entityB: Haitian revolutionaries had to defeat forces sent by France.

differences.entityA: The United States was recognized through the Treaty of Paris and eventually became economically powerful
differences.entityB: Haiti faced diplomatic isolation and was forced to pay reparations to France.

differences.entityA: The American Revolution primarily changed political control
differences.entityB: the Haitian Revolution also transformed the racial and social hierarchy.

differences.entityA: United States did not share this distinguishing feature to the same extent.
differences.entityB: Haiti became the first independent Black-led republic and the only state created through a successful large-scale slave revolt.

similarities.claim: Both began the period divided into multiple states rather than unified countries.
Both unified through nationalism, diplomacy, warfare, and Realpolitik.
Both were unified under the leadership of a particularly powerful state: Prussia in Germany and Piedmont-Sardinia in Italy.
Both fought against Austrian influence during the unification process.
Both became constitutional monarchies after unification.
Both participated in World War I.
Both experienced political dissatisfaction after World War I.

differences.entityA: German unification was led primarily by Otto von Bismarck and Prussia,
differences.entityB: Italian unification involved several leaders, including Cavour’s diplomacy, Garibaldi’s military campaigns, and Mazzini’s nationalist ideas.

differences.entityA: Bismarck wanted to preserve the authority of the Prussian monarchy
differences.entityB: Cavour supported a constitutional monarchy and liberal economic development.

differences.entityA: Germany unified primarily through Prussian military victories over Denmark, Austria, and France
differences.entityB: Italy used a combination of diplomacy, plebiscites, nationalist uprisings, and warfare.

differences.entityA: Germany became highly industrialized and a world leader in coal and steel
differences.entityB: Italy remained poorer and less industrialized.

differences.entityA: Poverty caused many Italians to immigrate to the United States and Argentina
differences.entityB: Germany’s expanding industrial economy attracted workers into growing cities.

differences.entityA: Germany fought with the Central Powers during World War I
differences.entityB: Italy joined the Allies.

differences.entityA: Germany was punished through the Treaty of Versailles and lost its monarchy
differences.entityB: Italy was on the winning side but was angry that it did not receive all the territory it had been promised.

similarities.claim: Both experienced major political transformations that produced new constitutional systems.
Both industrialized rapidly during the nineteenth century.
Both built modern militaries and expanded their territorial influence.
Both used transportation, education, and industrial development to strengthen national unity.
Both became imperial powers by the end of the nineteenth century.

differences.entityA: The United States gained independence from Britain,
differences.entityB: Japan remained sovereign but isolationist until the United States forced it to open to foreign trade.

differences.entityA: The United States became a federal republic
differences.entityB: Japan became a constitutional monarchy under the restored emperor.

differences.entityA: The United States industrialized especially rapidly after the Civil War
differences.entityB: Japan began rapid modernization after the 1868 Meiji Restoration.

differences.entityA: American industrialization relied heavily on private businesses, resources, and immigrant labor
differences.entityB: Japan initially used government-sponsored enterprises that were later sold to private zaibatsu.

differences.entityA: The United States expanded westward across North America, displacing Indigenous peoples
differences.entityB: Japan expanded its influence into East Asia.

differences.entityA: the United States abolished slavery after the Civil War.
differences.entityB: Japan abolished feudalism and the samurai class during the Meiji reforms

differences.entityA: The United States initiated Japan’s opening when Commodore Matthew Perry arrived with warships in 1853.
differences.entityB: Japan did not share this distinguishing feature to the same extent.

similarities.claim: Both were major industrial and military powers by the early twentieth century.
Both fought with the Allies during World War I.
Both competed for political and economic influence in the Pacific.
After World War II, both developed capitalist economies and became close allies.
Both became leading centers of technological development and global trade

differences.entityA: the United States increasingly opposed Japanese expansion.
differences.entityB: Japan pursued aggressive imperial expansion into Manchuria and China during the 1930s

differences.entityA: bringing the United States into World War II.
differences.entityB: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941

differences.entityA: The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima
differences.entityB: Nagasaki, contributing to Japan’s unconditional surrender.

differences.entityA: The United States emerged from World War II as a military superpower
differences.entityB: Japan was occupied, demilitarized, and rebuilt primarily as an economic power.

differences.entityA: The United States has a presidential federal republic
differences.entityB: Japan has a parliamentary constitutional monarchy.

differences.entityA: The United States maintains a large global military presence
differences.entityB: postwar Japan has placed greater constitutional restrictions on its use of military force.

differences.entityA: Relations were strained by Japanese immigration to the United States, resulting in the Gentlemen’s Agreement of 1907 and later immigration restrictions.
differences.entityB: Japan did not share this distinguishing feature to the same extent.

similarities.claim: Both were large, multiethnic land-based empires governed by ruling groups that represented only part of their populations.
Both experienced corruption, declining central authority, and difficulties governing large territories.
Both faced internal rebellions and nationalist movements.
Both were weakened by European military and economic interference.
Both attempted defensive modernization during the nineteenth century.
In both empires, conservative leaders resisted or reversed reforms.
Both failed to industrialize as successfully as Western Europe and Japan.
Both dynasties collapsed in the early twentieth century and were eventually replaced by republics.

differences.entityA: The Qing were Manchu rulers governing a predominantly Han Chinese population
differences.entityB: the Ottoman state was governed by a Turkish Muslim dynasty ruling numerous religious and ethnic groups.

differences.entityA: Qing government relied on Confucian bureaucracy and civil service examinations
differences.entityB: Ottoman government relied on Islamic and secular law, provincial officials, tax farming, and institutions such as the Janissaries.

differences.entityA: The Qing faced the Opium Wars and unequal treaties that opened Chinese ports and granted Europeans extraterritorial rights
differences.entityB: the Ottomans faced territorial losses, European intervention, and nationalist revolts, especially in the Balkans.

differences.entityA: Qing modernization centered on the Self-Strengthening Movement and Hundred Days of Reform
differences.entityB: Ottoman modernization centered on Mahmud II’s reforms and the Tanzimat reforms.

differences.entityA: Qing reformers attempted to introduce a constitutional monarchy, Western industry, and new medical and commercial systems
differences.entityB: Ottoman reforms secularized schools, codified laws, modernized the military, and expanded banking.

differences.entityA: The Boxer Rebellion targeted foreigners and Christians in China
differences.entityB: Ottoman nationalism and the Young Turk movement attempted to create a more unified state, often by suppressing ethnic differences.

differences.entityA: The Qing collapsed in 1911 and became the Republic of China
differences.entityB: the Ottoman Empire survived until its defeat in World War I and was formally replaced by the Republic of Turkey.

differences.entityA: China’s economy was heavily affected by tea, silver, and British opium imports
differences.entityB: the Ottoman economy suffered from tax farming, silver inflation, European competition, and growing financial dependence.

similarities.claim: Both emerged from World War II as global superpowers.
Both were permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.
Both developed nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missiles.
Both competed in the arms race and space race.
Both used propaganda to promote their political and economic systems.
Both created military and economic alliances.
Both avoided directly fighting each other, instead supporting opposing sides in proxy wars such as Korea, Vietnam, and Afghanistan.
Both relied on nuclear deterrence and mutually assured destruction to avoid direct war.
Periods of intense rivalry alternated with détente, when the two governments negotiated arms limits and reduced tensions.

differences.entityA: The United States supported capitalism, private property, and multiparty democracy
differences.entityB: the USSR supported communism, government ownership, and one-party rule.

differences.entityA: The United States promoted containment to prevent communism from spreading
differences.entityB: the USSR supported communist governments and revolutionary movements.

differences.entityA: The United States created NATO and the Marshall Plan
differences.entityB: the USSR created the Warsaw Pact and COMECON.

differences.entityA: The United States supported South Korea and South Vietnam
differences.entityB: the USSR supported North Korea and communist North Vietnam.

differences.entityA: The United States emerged from World War II with little physical damage
differences.entityB: the USSR lost millions of people and experienced widespread destruction.

differences.entityA: the United States generally exercised influence through alliances, military bases, and economic aid.
differences.entityB: The USSR established satellite governments in Eastern Europe

differences.entityA: The Soviet command economy emphasized heavy industry and collectivized agriculture,
differences.entityB: the American economy emphasized private enterprise and consumer production.

differences.entityA: the United States remained a unified global power.
differences.entityB: The Soviet Union collapsed in 1991,

similarities.claim: Both became communist states through revolutions led by communist parties.
Both established authoritarian, one-party governments.
Both censored the press and restricted political opposition.
Both attempted rapid industrialization through government economic planning.
Both collectivized agriculture and reduced private landownership.
Both prioritized heavy industry over consumer goods.
Both experienced catastrophic famines partly caused by government agricultural policies.
Both eventually introduced limited market reforms when strict communist policies damaged their economies.
China and the USSR were initially communist allies, but ideological and geopolitical disagreements produced the Sino-Soviet Split during the Cold War.

differences.entityA: The Bolsheviks took power in Russia in 1917
differences.entityB: the Chinese Communist Party defeated the Nationalists in 1949.

differences.entityA: The Russian Revolution was led by Lenin and later dominated by Stalin
differences.entityB: the Chinese Revolution was led by Mao Zedong.

differences.entityA: Mao based the Chinese communist movement heavily on peasant support
differences.entityB: Russian communism originally emphasized an urban working-class revolution.

differences.entityA: Stalin industrialized through Five-Year Plans and collectivized farms
differences.entityB: Mao launched the Great Leap Forward using rural communes and backyard steel production.

differences.entityA: Stalin’s collectivization contributed to famine in Ukraine
differences.entityB: Mao’s Great Leap Forward caused a much broader Chinese famine in which millions died.

differences.entityA: Stalin removed opponents through executions and gulags
differences.entityB: Mao mobilized young Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution to attack supposed enemies of communism.

differences.entityA: China did not establish an equivalent Eastern European-style bloc.
differences.entityB: The USSR controlled satellite states in Eastern Europe

differences.entityA: China’s Communist Party remained in power.
differences.entityB: The USSR collapsed in 1991,

differences.entityA: Deng Xiaoping introduced substantial private ownership, foreign investment, leased farms, and special economic zones
differences.entityB: maintaining strict political control.

differences.entityA: China increasingly followed its own Maoist path and competed with the USSR for influence.
differences.entityB: The USSR emphasized leadership of the international communist movement,

similarities.claim: Both were colonies of France.
Both developed strong nationalist independence movements after World War II.
Both gained independence through violent wars rather than peaceful negotiations.
Both used guerrilla warfare against French forces.
Both received foreign assistance for their independence movements.
Both nationalist movements adopted socialist ideas.
Both established authoritarian governments after independence.
Both experienced continued violence and political instability after colonial rule ended.

differences.entityA: Vietnam was part of French Indochina in Southeast Asia
differences.entityB: Algeria was a French settler colony in North Africa.

differences.entityA: Vietnam was occupied by Japan during World War II
differences.entityB: Algeria remained under French control.

differences.entityA: Vietnamese independence was led by Ho Chi Minh and the communist Viet Minh
differences.entityB: Algerian independence was led by the National Liberation Front, or FLN.

differences.entityA: Vietnam fought the First Indochina War from 1946 to 1954
differences.entityB: Algeria fought its independence war from 1954 to 1962.

differences.entityA: Vietnam defeated France decisively at Dien Bien Phu
differences.entityB: Algeria gained independence after prolonged warfare and Charles de Gaulle’s decision to permit Algerian self-rule.

differences.entityA: Vietnam was divided into communist North Vietnam and anti-communist South Vietnam after independence
differences.entityB: Algeria remained a single country.

differences.entityA: Vietnam became a major Cold War conflict involving extensive American intervention
differences.entityB: Algeria’s war primarily involved France, the FLN, and regional Arab support.

differences.entityA: Vietnam did not have a comparable European settler population.
differences.entityB: Algeria contained a large French settler population that left after independence, damaging its economy

differences.entityA: Vietnam was eventually reunified under communism
differences.entityB: Algeria later experienced a civil war between the government and Islamist opposition.

similarities.claim: Both were colonies that gained independence during the post–World War II decolonization period.
Both independence movements were led by influential nationalist leaders.
Kwame Nkrumah and Ho Chi Minh both linked independence to broader political ideologies.
Both countries attempted to reduce the influence of their former colonial powers.
Both experienced authoritarian government after independence.
Both were affected by the political pressures of the Cold War.

differences.entityA: Ghana was a British colony
differences.entityB: Vietnam was a French colony that was also occupied by Japan.

differences.entityA: Ghana negotiated its independence peacefully in 1957
differences.entityB: Vietnam fought France in the First Indochina War.

differences.entityA: Ghanaian independence was led by Kwame Nkrumah
differences.entityB: Vietnamese independence was led by Ho Chi Minh.

differences.entityA: Nkrumah promoted Pan-Africanism and African political unity
differences.entityB: Ho Chi Minh used communism as a vehicle for Vietnamese nationalism.

differences.entityA: Ghana remained territorially united
differences.entityB: Vietnam was divided into communist North Vietnam and anti-communist South Vietnam.

differences.entityA: Ghana did not become a major Cold War battlefield
differences.entityB: Vietnam became the site of an extensive proxy war involving the United States, USSR, and China.

differences.entityA: Nkrumah was removed in a military coup in 1966
differences.entityB: Ho Chi Minh’s communist movement eventually defeated South Vietnam and reunified the country.

differences.entityA: Ghana’s post-independence problems centered on debt, corruption, and military intervention
differences.entityB: Vietnam’s centered on prolonged warfare, land redistribution, and national reunification.

similarities.claim: Both were colonies of Britain.
Both developed organized nationalist movements.
Both negotiated independence rather than defeating Britain in a prolonged colonial war.
Both gained independence shortly after World War II.
Both had charismatic nationalist leaders: Gandhi and Nehru in India, and Nkrumah in Ghana.
Both supported greater cooperation among formerly colonized countries.
Both attempted economic and social reforms after independence.
Both faced challenges caused by colonial economic structures.

differences.entityA: India became independent in 1947
differences.entityB: Ghana became independent in 1957.

differences.entityA: India’s movement used mass civil disobedience and nonviolent resistance
differences.entityB: Ghana’s independence resulted more directly from political negotiation with Britain.

differences.entityA: India was partitioned into India and Pakistan, producing widespread religious violence and migration
differences.entityB: Ghana was not partitioned.

differences.entityA: Indian nationalism had to manage major Hindu-Muslim divisions
differences.entityB: Ghanaian nationalism emphasized Pan-African identity and resistance to colonial rule.

differences.entityA: India established a lasting multiparty parliamentary democracy
differences.entityB: Nkrumah increasingly restricted opposition and became a dictator.

differences.entityA: India maintained civilian rule.
differences.entityB: Ghana experienced a military coup that removed Nkrumah in 1966

differences.entityA: India became a leader of the Non-Aligned Movement
differences.entityB: Nkrumah focused especially on Pan-Africanism and helped establish the Organization of African Unity.

differences.entityA: India’s post-independence land reforms had mixed success
differences.entityB: Ghana’s government was particularly criticized for debt and corruption.

similarities.claim: Both were African colonies that gained independence after World War II.
Both independence movements were based on nationalism and opposition to European rule.
Both established governments led by the main nationalist independence movement.
Both adopted some socialist policies after independence.
Both developed authoritarian political systems.
Both experienced coups, instability, or violence after independence.
Both remained economically affected by their former colonial relationships.

differences.entityA: Ghana was controlled by Britain
differences.entityB: Algeria was controlled by France.

differences.entityA: Ghana negotiated independence peacefully in 1957
differences.entityB: Algeria gained independence in 1962 after an eight-year war.

differences.entityA: Ghanaian independence was led by Kwame Nkrumah
differences.entityB: Algerian independence was led by the FLN.

differences.entityA: Nkrumah promoted Pan-Africanism
differences.entityB: the FLN received support from Egypt and other Arab countries.

differences.entityA: Ghana did not have a large European settler population
differences.entityB: Algeria contained a substantial French population that strongly resisted independence.

differences.entityA: Ghana’s independence struggle involved political organization and negotiation
differences.entityB: Algeria’s involved guerrilla warfare and hundreds of thousands of deaths.

differences.entityA: Ghana’s government was overthrown in a military coup in 1966
differences.entityB: Algeria’s FLN remained dominant and established a socialist authoritarian state.

differences.entityA: Ghana did not experience a directly comparable conflict.
differences.entityB: Algeria later experienced a major civil war after the military cancelled an election won by an Islamist party

differences.entityA: Ghana’s major economic problems included government debt and corruption
differences.entityB: Algeria suffered when departing French settlers took skills and investment with them.

similarities.claim: Both emerged from territories previously controlled by Britain shortly after World War II.
Both were shaped by competing nationalist movements seeking separate states.
Both underwent partition largely because different religious and national communities feared being ruled by another group.
Both partitions produced widespread violence and large-scale population displacement.
Both immediately faced conflict with neighboring states created or affected by the partition.
Both continued to experience territorial disputes after independence: India over Kashmir and Israel over Palestinian territories and neighboring Arab lands.

World War II accelerated both developments: Indian demands for independence grew after millions of Indians served Britain, while the Holocaust increased international support for establishing a Jewish homeland.

differences.entityA: Israel was created from part of the British Mandate of Palestine under a United Nations partition plan.
differences.entityB: India was an established British colony that gained independence,

differences.entityA: Palestine was proposed to be divided into Jewish and Arab states, but the proposed Arab Palestinian state was not successfully established in 1948.
differences.entityB: British India was divided into the independent states of Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan

differences.entityA: Israel’s creation followed Zionist migration, international diplomacy, the UN partition decision, and warfare.
differences.entityB: India’s independence movement relied heavily on mass organization, boycotts, and nonviolent civil disobedience led by figures such as Gandhi and Nehru

differences.entityA: Israel declared independence and immediately fought neighboring Arab states.
differences.entityB: India became independent through negotiations with Britain, although partition caused severe communal violence

differences.entityA: Israel became a Jewish-majority state.
differences.entityB: India became a secular, Hindu-majority democratic republic

differences.entityA: the Arab-Israeli War caused many Palestinians to flee or be displaced into refugee camps.
differences.entityB: The partition of India caused Hindus and Sikhs to migrate toward India and Muslims toward Pakistan

differences.entityA: Pakistan later divided when East Pakistan became Bangladesh in 1971
differences.entityB: Bangladesh was not part of the original 1947 partition as a separate country.

differences.entityA: the Israeli-Palestinian conflict involved competing Jewish and Palestinian Arab claims to the same territory, rather than simply Judaism versus Islam.
differences.entityB: India’s central conflict was primarily between advocates of a united India and those demanding a separate Muslim state
